# k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster (Resource)

A Kubernetes cluster, created from a ClusterType in a project.

Requires `region` and `project`, on the provider block or on this resource. Create, scale and destroy are asynchronous on the platform; this resource waits for each to settle, bounded by its `timeouts` block. Create and delete default to `3h`, the rest to the provider's `operation_timeout`.

A wait that times out, or a run that is interrupted, does not stop the operation, which keeps running on the platform. A create that stops waiting fails, and Terraform taints the cluster. Run `terraform untaint` on it and then `terraform apply`, which waits for the same cluster. A plan that would replace it instead warns before the approval, in whatever state the platform reports, that applying it cancels what's still being built, or deletes the cluster, and creates it again. `terraform destroy` runs that plan first to refresh state, so it shows the warning too, and then only deletes. A failed cluster's delete can fail too. A create of an `id` the platform holds for a cluster without this provider's create token, such as one made outside Terraform, is refused unless `allow_replace = true`. One with the token passes, since only an apply can tell whether this state holds it: if another state does, the create fails with "already exists" and nothing is deleted. A destroy that stops waiting leaves the cluster in state, and the next `terraform destroy` waits for the same delete without sending another. A tainted cluster without the token, such as an imported one, refuses `terraform destroy` too, since destroy runs that plan first: run `terraform untaint` on it, then `terraform destroy`. If the state doesn't hold it, `terraform destroy -refresh=false` skips that plan. A run killed before the create returns, such as by `kill -9` or a lost CI runner, saves nothing, so the cluster keeps being built with nothing in state: `terraform destroy` finds nothing to destroy, and the next apply fails with "already exists" and gives the `terraform import` that takes it back.

The platform deletes a cluster only once nothing is running on it, so destroying one that is still `creating` or `updating` cancels that operation first and warns that it did, all within the delete timeout. A plan that destroys the cluster, or replaces one that isn't tainted, warns before the approval too when the last refresh saw the operation, because an operation cancelled that way does not finish: a cancelled upgrade leaves the cluster `failed`. A plan that replaces a tainted cluster warns from the platform's read, since Terraform doesn't show the provider the tainted one. Only a destroy cancels an operation, the one that starts an apply replacing the cluster included, and `on_destroy_busy = "wait"` makes a destroy wait for the operation to finish instead. To cancel it and keep the cluster, invoke the `k0rdent_cluster_cancel_operation` action.

**What replaces it.** Changing `cluster_type`, `id`, `project`, `region` or `ssh_access` cannot be done in place and replaces the cluster. A cluster runs tenant workloads, and a replacement deletes it, its nodes and everything scheduled on them before a new, empty cluster is created. So a plan that would replace it fails and names the attribute, unless `allow_replace = true` is set on the resource. Everything else changes in place.

## Example Usage

```terraform
data "k0rdent_cluster_type" "gpu" {
  id = "gpu-training"
}

resource "k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster" "training" {
  id           = "training-01"
  cluster_type = data.k0rdent_cluster_type.gpu.self_link
  display_name = "Training cluster"

  node_pool = {
    gpu-workers = {
      node_count = 4
    }
  }

  # Merged with the provider's `default_tags` into `tags_all`. These win.
  tags = {
    team = "research"
  }

  # Set when nodes are built. Changing it replaces the cluster, which
  # needs `allow_replace = true`.
  ssh_access = [
    {
      username        = "ops"
      ssh_public_keys = [trimspace(file("~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub"))]
      sudo            = "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    },
  ]

  timeouts {
    create = "45m"
  }
}

# Pinned to a version. Change `version_id` to a later one to upgrade in place.
# The update timeout covers the whole upgrade.
data "k0rdent_cluster_type_version" "inference" {
  cluster_type = "gpu-inference"
  version_id   = "aaaaaaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000004"
}

resource "k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster" "inference" {
  id           = "inference-01"
  cluster_type = data.k0rdent_cluster_type_version.inference.self_link

  timeouts {
    update = "2h"
  }
}

# Security groups on the cluster, applied in list order. Leave
# `security_groups` out to leave them alone, or set `[]` to remove them all.
resource "k0rdent_security_group" "api" {
  id = "api-from-office"

  ingress {
    action             = "permit"
    protocol           = "tcp"
    source_prefix      = "203.0.113.0/24"
    destination_prefix = "0.0.0.0/0"

    destination_port_range = "6443"
  }
}

resource "k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster" "filtered" {
  id           = "filtered-01"
  cluster_type = data.k0rdent_cluster_type.gpu.self_link

  security_groups = [k0rdent_security_group.api.id]
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `cluster_type` (String) Reference to the ClusterType to create this cluster from, as returned in a cluster type's `self_link`, for example `/v1/regions/us-texas-1/compute/cluster-types/gpu-training`. The `/versions/{id}` segment is optional: omit it to bind the ClusterType's current version, include it to pin one. Both a path and an absolute URL are accepted. Changing it to another ClusterType replaces the cluster.

Pinning a later `available` version of the same ClusterType upgrades the cluster in place, one version per step: the plan says how many steps it takes, and the apply waits out each before the next, skipping any `draft` or `deprecated` version between. The update timeout bounds the whole apply. If a step fails, the apply stops, state records the version the cluster reached, and nothing is deleted; the platform does not retry an upgrade from `failed`.

Node count changes in the same apply are made before or after each step, wherever the versions' node pool bounds admit them, since a scale is checked against the version the cluster is on and an upgrade against the one it moves to. The plan fails when no order works, and for an earlier version, one that is not `available`, a version the ClusterType does not have, or a BMaaS-only version in the way. See `cluster_type_resolved` for what the platform bound. **Known gap.** A tenant can't read the hardware or the image behind a ClusterType's machine types, so choosing a ClusterType for its hardware means writing one an operator named. The [hardcoded values](../guides/hardcoded-values.md) guide names the side that has to change. **Can force replacement** (needs `allow_replace = true`): replaced only when the new reference names a different ClusterType; another version of the same one is upgraded in place or refused. **Constraints:** Must be a ClusterType reference whose version, when it names one, is a UUID.
- `id` (String) Cluster name, the one the platform shows, and the id this resource is imported by. Lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. Required, so that a plan can read it before creating it: a create that stopped waiting leaves it still being built, and the plan that would replace it warns so, with the way to wait for it instead. **Forces replacement** (needs `allow_replace = true`). **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL. String length must be at most 63.

### Optional

- `allow_replace` (Boolean) Permit a plan that replaces this cluster. Left out or `false`, a change that cannot be made in place fails the plan, naming the attribute that forces the replacement, instead of destroying the cluster and creating another. Set it to `true` in the same configuration as the change to let the replacement go ahead, and remove it afterwards to put the guard back. It is read from the configuration being planned and must be known at plan time. It is never sent to the platform: setting or removing it on its own is an update that changes nothing there.
- `description` (String) Free-form description. Mutable.
- `display_name` (String) Human-friendly name. Mutable.
- `node_pool` (Attributes Map) Per-pool node counts, keyed by the ClusterType node pool's id.

This is a **sparse override set**, not the full pool list. The platform materializes one pool for every pool on the bound ClusterType version, using each pool's default count where this map does not name it, so naming one pool here does not remove the others. A pool named here is managed by Terraform: changing its count scales the cluster. A pool left out is left to the ClusterType's default and is not drift-checked.

Omit the attribute entirely and the platform's materialized counts are read into state as-is. **Known gap.** A pool's machine type is readable only as a name, not as hardware, so choosing a pool for its hardware means writing its id as a literal. The [hardcoded values](../guides/hardcoded-values.md) guide names the side that has to change. **Constraints:** Each pool id must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, not ending with a hyphen, and at most 63 characters long. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--node_pool))
- `on_destroy_busy` (String) What a destroy does when the cluster is `creating` or `updating`, which the platform refuses to delete. `cancel`, the default when unset, cancels the running operation and then deletes the cluster. Whatever that operation was doing doesn't finish, and a cancelled upgrade leaves the cluster `failed`. `wait` waits for the operation to finish and then deletes the cluster, within the delete timeout. If another operation starts in the meantime, it waits for that one too. An operation that outlasts the timeout fails the destroy with nothing deleted, so a cluster wedged mid-operation needs `cancel`.

Never sent to the platform. A destroy reads it from state, like `timeouts`, so change it in an apply before the destroy that should use it. That apply sends nothing and doesn't wait, even while the cluster is mid-operation. A create that stops waiting or fails records it, so the destroy of that cluster follows it too. To change it on a tainted cluster, run `terraform untaint` on the cluster first: otherwise the apply plans a new cluster in its place, and the destroy of this one reads the value already in state. **Constraints:** Value must be one of: ["cancel" "wait"].
- `on_failed` (String) What a plan does with a cluster the platform reports `failed`. `wait`, the default when unset, plans an update and warns with the platform's reason: the apply waits up to 2m for the platform to bring the cluster back to `active`, and fails, deleting nothing, if it doesn't. `keep` warns and plans nothing, for a cluster you keep as it is, such as one whose upgrade failed: the platform doesn't scale or upgrade a `failed` cluster, though its `tags`, `display_name` and `description` can still change. A cluster left `failed` by the `k0rdent_cluster_cancel_operation` action plans nothing either way.

Never sent to the platform. **Constraints:** Value must be one of: ["wait" "keep"].
- `project` (String) Project this resource belongs to. Defaults to the provider's `project`. It's part of the resource's API path, so a resource can't move between projects. **Forces replacement** (needs `allow_replace = true`). **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL.
- `region` (String) Region this resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `region`. It's part of the resource's API path, so a resource can't move between regions. **Forces replacement** (needs `allow_replace = true`). **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL.
- `security_groups` (List of String) Ids of the security groups that filter this cluster's machines, in the order the fabric applies them. Order is significant: a group listed earlier takes precedence over one listed later, so reordering the list is a change. At most 16, each named once.

Changing the list updates the cluster in place: the provider sends the new list on its own and waits for the cluster to settle. The cluster is never replaced for it.

**Leaving it out and writing `[]` differ.** Left out, the provider sends nothing, never detaches anything, and reads whatever groups the platform reports into state without treating them as drift. Removing the attribute from a configuration that had set it therefore leaves the groups attached. Written as `[]`, the provider detaches every group on the cluster, including any attached outside Terraform.

The platform answers 422 when an id is unknown or in another project, when it names a VPC's platform-managed default group, or when no node pool on the cluster type has an interface on a network in a `nico`-backed VPC for the groups to go on. A group a cluster holds can't be deleted until it is detached.

These groups filter the machines' network interfaces, not the Kubernetes API address. **Constraints:** List must contain at most 16 elements. All values must be unique. Each security group id must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, not ending with a hyphen, and from 1 to 63 characters long.
- `ssh_access` (Attributes Set) Linux users written onto every node when the cluster is provisioned, each with the public keys allowed to log in as that user. Up to 32 users. Only public keys go here. Keys reach a node as it's provisioned, so SSH answers before the cluster is `active`.

A refresh reads the users the platform reports, so an import fills this in and a difference from the configuration shows in the plan. Where the platform doesn't report them, state keeps what the provider sent.

**Changing it replaces the cluster**, because the platform won't change a running cluster's users. Leaving it out and `[]` both mean no users, so moving between them replaces nothing. Where the platform doesn't report the users, a cluster that was imported, or created by an earlier version of the provider, has no record of them: a change is recorded without replacing anything, the nodes keep the users they have, and the plan warns. Use `terraform apply -replace` to put new users on such a cluster's nodes. **Can force replacement** (needs `allow_replace = true`): replaced when it changes, unless state has no record of the nodes' users. **Constraints:** Set must contain at most 32 elements. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--ssh_access))
- `storage_ceiling_gib` (Number) Storage the cluster declares, in GiB. It's charged against the organization's and the project's `storage_gib` quota, and isn't enforced on the storage array. From 1 to 1048576.

It can be raised in place and never lowered: a lower value is refused at plan time, since the platform refuses it too. Left out, the cluster keeps whatever ceiling it has, and removing it from configuration doesn't clear it. A raise is sent once the cluster is `active`, and one refused while the cluster or its quota accounting is settling is sent again after the cluster settles. A raise past a quota is refused with the amount that would be admitted. **Constraints:** Value must be between 1 and 1048576.
- `tags` (Map of String) User-defined labels. Mutable. **Constraints:** The key `terraform-provider-k0rdent/create-token` is the provider's own.
- `timeouts` (Block, Optional) How long each operation may take before it fails. Left out, `create` and `delete` default to `3h` and every other operation to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--timeouts))

### Read-Only

- `cluster_type_resolved` (String) The `clusterType` value the platform returned, verbatim. It may differ from `cluster_type`: the platform may resolve an unversioned reference to a pinned `/versions/{id}` one, and it may answer with a path where an absolute URL was given. This attribute exists so that resolution is visible in state rather than hidden by the provider's comparison.
- `kubernetes_version` (String) The Kubernetes version the bound ClusterType version carries, such as `v1.35.1+k0s.0`, read from that version's `k8s.k0sVersion`. It's read-only: the platform versions a cluster by its ClusterType version and ignores a declared Kubernetes version, so pinning `cluster_type` to a later version is how it changes. A plan that upgrades shows the version the upgrade reaches. It's the version the cluster is bound to, not a reading of what runs: while an upgrade rolls out, the `k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster` data source's `control_plane_version` is what the control plane runs. Null when the bound version carries no Kubernetes configuration, or the platform no longer finds it.
- `node_count` (Number) Total nodes across every materialized pool, as reported by the platform.
- `self_link` (String) Platform-defined reference to this cluster.
- `state` (String) Lifecycle state as last read. This resource waits for a settled state, so it is normally `active`. A plan on a cluster the platform reports `failed` warns with the platform's reason, and plans an update that waits for the cluster to come back unless `on_failed` is `keep`.
- `tags_all` (Map of String) Every tag the platform holds for this resource: the provider's `default_tags` with this resource's own `tags` on top, a resource tag winning over a default with the same key. Known at plan whenever both are, so the plan shows the result. The provider's create token never appears here.
- `vpc` (String) Id of the VPC this cluster brought with it. Name the VPC through this rather than a data source: it stays known while the cluster changes, so a peering or a security-group binding that names it is not replaced. A peering takes it as `vpc`, and a peering in this project that points at it takes it as `remote_vpc`.

<a id="nestedatt--node_pool"></a>
### Nested Schema for `node_pool`

Required:

- `node_count` (Number) Number of nodes in this pool. Must lie within the ClusterType pool's `node_count_min` and `node_count_max` where those are set. **Constraints:** Value must be at least 0.


<a id="nestedatt--ssh_access"></a>
### Nested Schema for `ssh_access`

Required:

- `ssh_public_keys` (List of String) Public keys, each one `authorized_keys` line, allowed to log in as this user. From 1 to 32. The platform accepts `ssh-ed25519`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521`, `ssh-rsa` of at least 2048 bits, and the `sk-` security-key variants. Kept in the order written. A key must not start or end with whitespace, since the platform trims it: read one from a file with `trimspace(file(...))`, because `file()` keeps the trailing newline. **Constraints:** Must hold from 1 to 32 keys. Each key must be one line with no whitespace at either end, and at most 16384 characters long. Read one from a file with `trimspace(file(...))`.
- `username` (String) Linux username to provision on every host. Must match `^[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$`. **Constraints:** Must start with a lowercase letter or an underscore, then up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, underscores or hyphens.

Optional:

- `display_name` (String) Human-friendly name for this entry. **Constraints:** String length must be at most 255.
- `sudo` (String) A sudo fragment granting this user privileges, such as `ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL`. **Constraints:** String length must be at most 4096.

### Nested Schema for `timeouts`

Optional:

- `create` (String) Bounds the whole create, including the wait until the platform reports it ready. Left out, it defaults to `3h`, or to the provider's `operation_timeout` once the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.
- `delete` (String) Bounds the whole destroy, including the wait until the platform reports it gone. Left out, it defaults to `3h`, or to the provider's `operation_timeout` once the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.
- `update` (String) Bounds the whole update, including the wait until the platform settles. Left out, it defaults to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.

## Timeouts

The `timeouts` block sets how long each operation may take before it fails:

- `create` (default `3h`). Bounds the whole create, including the wait until the platform reports it ready.
- `update` (default `2h`). Bounds the whole update, including the wait until the platform settles.
- `delete` (default `3h`). Bounds the whole destroy, including the wait until the platform reports it gone.

A create or a delete builds or frees hardware, which can take more than 2 hours, so it defaults to `3h`. Every other default is the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. Once it's set, it's every operation's default, these two included. A value of zero or less is refused at plan time rather than read as no limit.

A wait that runs out, or a run that is interrupted, stops nothing on the platform. A create that stops waiting fails, and Terraform taints the object: run `terraform untaint` on it and then `terraform apply`, which waits for the same object. A delete that stops waiting fails and stays in state, and the next `terraform destroy` waits for the same delete without sending another.

```terraform
resource "k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster" "example" {
  # ...

  timeouts {
    create = "45m"
    update = "45m"
    delete = "45m"
  }
}
```

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

In Terraform v1.12.0 and later, the [`import` block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import) can be used with the `identity` attribute, for example:

```terraform
# The same address with each part named. Leave out region and project to
# use the provider's.
import {
  to = k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster.example
  identity = {
    region  = "us-texas-1"
    project = "cp-production"
    id      = "my-cluster"
  }
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
### Identity Schema

#### Required

- `id` (String) The resource's id.

#### Optional

- `project` (String) Project the resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `project` on import.
- `region` (String) Region the resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `region` on import.

In Terraform v1.5.0 and later, the [`import` block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import) can be used with the `id` attribute, for example:

```terraform
# Takes every id form `terraform import` does. The first command below uses
# the provider's region and project, the second names them. If you name them,
# set both in the resource block too, or the next plan replaces the cluster.
#
# The import adopts every node pool. If node_pool names only some, the next
# plan shows an in-place update that changes nothing on the platform.
import {
  to = k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster.example
  id = "us-texas-1/cp-production/my-cluster"
}
```

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
terraform import k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster.example my-cluster

terraform import k0rdent_kubernetes_cluster.example us-texas-1/cp-production/my-cluster
```
